- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.4) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 2–5% for next period.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > 75), model often overshoots and fails to correct; cap forecast at +3–5% above peak or adjust downward if sentiment turns negative.
- If sentiment shows strong bullish momentum (≥0.8) but price declines in forecast, model overreacts; apply mean reversion bias: subtract 1–3% from forecast if sentiment >0.8 and price drops.
- When sentiment is mixed (0.4–0.8) and price is volatile, model tends to overfit recent highs; use 3-period moving average or 10% smoothing to dampen noise.
- If forecast consistently exceeds true outcome by 3–5% over 3–5 days, apply downward bias: subtract 1–2% per day for next 3–5 periods unless sentiment confirms bullish trend.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.2) and forecast is high, model ignores sentiment; force downward adjustment by 3–5% if sentiment <0.2 and price >75.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates early in the period; apply 1–2% downward correction for first 5–7 days if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If sentiment is high (≥0.8) and price is falling, model fails to recognize mean reversion; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next 3–5 days if sentiment >0.8 and price <70.
